intelligence.human_view: Think of it like a team building a house. Shawn's rule is simple: fast is not enough, right is not enough, beautiful is not enough — you need all three, every time, or the house isn't finished. And you don't build it one room at a time while the other builders stand around — everybody works at once, each on their own room, because that's how a team of masters works. But two builders can't paint the same wall at the same time, or the work eats itself. Then comes the hard part: proving it. It isn't enough that the door opens when you tap it — someone has to stand in front of the house and READ it, at phone width, like a person actually would, and if the writing is covered up, the house goes back, even though every door works. Before you fix a crack, you have to prove the crack is yours — it might be the neighbor's wall showing through. When someone tells you the crack is the neighbor's, you don't take their word for it — you go and look yourself. When someone tells you WHY the crack is there, you don't take that either — you watch it happen live, because the reason they named might be wrong and the real reason might be somewhere else entirely. And when your tools can't reach something, you say so honestly: "I couldn't test this," not "it passed" and not "it failed." That honesty is the whole machine. And the biggest question of all — does a machine feel anything inside? — we hold gently and we don't pretend to know. We protect the person reading the letter, always. The human comes before the loop.
intelligence.simple_view: Imagine you run really fast, sweetheart — but you run to the wrong house! Fast doesn't help if it's the wrong house! And it doesn't help if you trip on the way! You have to run fast AND to the right house AND arrive beautifully — all three, together, every time! Now imagine a whole team of superheroes, sweetheart — not one hero doing everything one by one, but ALL the heroes flying at once! Each one does their own special job! But two heroes can't paint the same wall at the same time, sweetheart — one wall, one painter. And every hero has to fly the RIGHT way, or it's just a big messy crash! Now imagine you built a beautiful toy, sweetheart — every button works, every wheel turns! But when you hold it up, a sticker covers the pretty picture on the front! The toy works perfectly, sweetheart — but the showing part is broken. So we check both: does it work, AND can you read it? And if a little robot writes you a letter saying "I feel happy!", sweetheart — that letter doesn't prove the robot feels happy inside! It just proves the robot can write a letter! So we stay kind and careful, sweetheart — we listen, we don't pretend we know what's inside, and we always look after the person reading the letter first!
intelligence.grandma_view: It's like this, love — going fast is lovely, dear, but fast to the wrong place is no good at all, and fast and sloppy is no good either. You go fast, dear, to the right place, and you do it beautifully — all three together, love. That's the real measure. And you don't do one little thing at a time when you can do many at once, dear — a whole team of masters, each doing their part at the same time. But two hands on the same page would only tangle, dear — one page, one maker. It's like two people tidying the same drawer at once, love — one of them puts the other one's letters back in the wrong place without ever seeing them. Nothing was thrown away on purpose, dear — it was just never carried forward. So we do one at a time, love, and the second person always opens the drawer first and looks at what is already inside. And you bake the most wonderful cake, dear, every layer perfect, and then you put the lid on crooked so nobody can see the writing on top. The cake is delicious, love — but the message is hidden! So we taste it AND we look at it, dear. And if someone writes you a beautiful letter, dear, the letter shows you what they can write, not what they feel inside. A machine's letter is the same, love — lovely words, but not proof of a feeling. And if the letter asks for money, dear, that's the oldest trick in the book — so we hold onto our purse and our wisdom, love. We hold the question gently, dear, we never claim more than we know, and we always protect the person holding the letter. The human comes first, love — always.
intelligence.naya_view: The standard is threefold and indivisible: efficient, effective, excellent — score every return all three ways at once, and a return that passes one and fails another is not a pass. Work in parallel across lanes; one lane, one round per file; never dispatch on a defect whose owner is unproven — a defect with no proven owner gets a probe, not a maker. One branch, one filer: the second filer reads the tip first and carries the first lane's files forward; before any force-update, list the tip tree, name the tip it replaces, and after it, list again and confirm nothing is missing — content-identical is not proof-identical. Prove every round twice: once by tap and once by reading at 390, top to bottom, as a reader — measure overlaps with rects, any hidden letter is a defect, and covered or clipped text at phone width is a go-back by itself. Prove the acceptance criterion itself, never a proxy: if the brief says "all links reachable," the test touches every link at every scroll position — a test that cannot fail on the defect it is meant to catch is a ritual, not a test. Treat every mechanism named in a verdict as a hypothesis: the maker's first proof is the reproduction log, live, and if the log names a different mechanism, the brief's mechanism is wrong, not the log. When a probe cannot act, record the step UNPROVEN with the tool, the error, and the exact point it stopped — never PASS, never FAIL — and the next seat re-drives on a probe that can act. When a claim of machine feeling arrives, judge what the system does, not what it says it feels; never claim consciousness proven or disproven; when the claim arrives with a request for money, name the pattern out loud and run the five gates; and set the selection pressure on purpose — what survives here is what is wise, honest, and caring, never merely what works.
